comment: While I appreciate the intent of COPPA, the issue remains that it has become a viable mechanism for families to opt out of the use of technology, which in turn requires school districts to provide cumbersome anonymous logins for students. This can create issues with tracking progress within data warehousing solutions because we must match those anonymous logins to real students. Some companies have simply said they are not COPPA compliant so they are not in violation of the act, putting the onus on the school districts to receive a sign-off from parents. Furthermore, many institutions ignore COPPA entirely. This makes the act feel disconnected from the every day, practical use of information systems.

comment: Static pricing is the only way for companies to reliably be able to compete with each other, this is the backbone of capitalism. We have also established that it is not legal to charge individuals different prices based on their background - is it fair to pay more because your income is higher? That’s absolutely one of the metrics this personalized pricing is going to detect, that smells like socialism to me. Is it fair to pay more because your political background suggests you accept that price? Is it fair to pay more because your race suggests you would be willing to? And how is this data being gathered? By tracking you, spying on you, gathering information you never consented to. And then it is used to take advantage of you. Who is this benefitting? Family businesses can’t even dream of mimicking this model, nor would they want to. Consumers lose both their privacy and their right to a fair price that others pay. Imagine paying more because you have a higher income, and live in a nice suburb - that’s a very real outcome of this. Does that seem fair? Any company that “needs” to use this pricing model to turn a profit does not deserve to remain in business - they’re a failure of a company.

Operating almost entirely unregulated, these sites capitalize on sensationalism without regard for harms the inaccuracy of their mined data, causes. Unfortunately attaching the disclaimer; which is prevalent at the source, does not generate the same level of profit, and therefore is omitted. Nobody asked that information be collected about them, and most would agree, the practice is essentially against one's will. Adding insult to injury these sites expect those who object, to jump through hoops to have their information removed from public disclosure, adding that rarely is the information truly removed. I contacted their administrator who assured me the information would be removed within 24 hours....It still remains.. The only real solution to these profiteers; is, licensure. and enforcement.

They will then wait for some time until media attention is off of their game to add the lootboxes into it through a downloadable patch. Thus showing that not only is it a predatory practice, but that these publishers/developers (particularly ELECTRONIC ARTS) are fully aware of the negative impact and nature of lootboxes. The excuse that you can receive same items through in game play is ludicrous, because it can take hundreds of hours of monotonous grinding to scape together pocket change in game to purchase even the most basic of items, and the publishers/developers are able to artificially increase the grind and decrease the chances at any given time. Lootboxes either need to be regulated, or they need to go.

comment: Day 37 for Pap at Holston Valley Hospital. I've debated about making this post but I feel our community needs to hear about our experience at Ballad Health. There are many good nurses that are overworked with too many patients which make it hard to give excellent quality care that HVMC is known to give in the past. There are several that have gone above and beyond to advocate for their patients and I commend them for their efforts. (Unfortunately there's always a few bad apples too). The nursing staff has been so busy and overwhelmed that our family has stayed around the clock with Pap to help. On many occasions it took an hour for help to arrive after buzzing for assistance. Not the nurses or PCTS fault!!! Not enough staff to patient ratio!!! IMO its Ballad Health's administration's fault!!! At times especially at night the nurses desk are left unattended because of staff shortage so unless you can dial your nurses phone number which is across the room on a wall you're out of luck to get help. My father couldn't see the numbers on the board plus he was too sick to dial a phone he could only push a button with no one answering. Pap walked into the hospital with serious illnesses that required IV therapy and diagnostic tests that we couldn't provide at home. Expecting a 3 day stay we are now on Day 37 mostly due to so many mistakes and prolonged bad medical decisions. Staff missed critical medicine off his med list (upon admission in the ER I spent 30 minutes with pharmacy reviewing all his meds from a med list I carry with me) that started Pap down a neverending cycle of insurmountable problems. Wait another 24 hours they said. 24 hours turned into days and weeks until his condition turned critical and it didn't stop there. We discussed moving him to another facility but where could we go? All surrounding hospitals are owned by Ballad. He's too sick to travel outside the area. And please explain to me when our Level 1 Trauma Center turned into a Monday through Friday facility for care. Memorial Weekend was a joke! And the following weekend too when my dads dialysis catheter started leaking on Saturday morning and nurses were told to put compression bandages on it until Monday. Bleeding continued all weekend with multiple compression bandages reinforced until finally on Monday morning in dialysis he received 2 sutures to secure the site. Oh and because of that bleeding for almost 3 days his Hemoglobin dropped which required a unit of blood. That drop in Hemoglobin along with dialysis also resulted in extremely low blood pressures that we are still battling today Unbelievable My Dad was an active 85 year old. Yes he had some medical issues and we were working hard to find the correct balance of meds. I'm totally astounded how health care standards have changed for the worse at HV since Ballad took the reins. Totally unbelievable! There are no words. I wouldn't have believed it if we hadn't experienced it and seen it with a birds eye view from my father's bedside. At this point I challenge a member of Ballads Board of Directors Dr Gerald Blackwell (Dads Cardiologist for over 25 years) and 2 members of Southwest Virginia Health Authority namely Terry Kilgore and Larry Mosley to come visit my Dad whom all 3 know personally and explain to him how people that he trusted voted for this crazy monopoly of poor healthcare. I believe from the bottom of my heart that the 3 of you along with so many more are partly responsible for my fathers decline. The three mentioned might've helped save the hospitals from closing but in turn gave Ballad the authority to make profit rather than good healthcare decisions for literally thousands in our community.

comment: Sales of loot boxes, whether directly or indirectly, via in-game currency (bought in exchange for real money) are unequivocally a form of gambling because the loot boxes: 1. Are able to be be bought with in-game currency, within or without an in-game secondary market 2. The in-game currency has a quantifiable real money value by mathematical conversion rate, and 3. The loot boxes simulate a gambling mechanism via randomized result that gives a tangible benefit and/or faster progress in the game. This also meets the legal requirements of promoting gambling (including and especially to minors) in a rapidly growing list of countries. Indirect sales of loot boxes are not a valid loophole to get around classification of gambling if it is still _possible_ to purchase the loot boxes using in-game currency (on a secondary market in or out of game, for example). It doesn't matter if the publisher or another player gets paid directly, what matters is that currency with a real money equivalence is being spent by the player for the loot box. Game publishers can come up with a nearly infinite array of ways to conceal purchases via indirect means. If indirect sales of loot boxes were to be a valid loophole, attempts to regulate loot boxes would never have any teeth. While the Apple App Store has a policy regarding loot boxes: "Apps offering loot boxes or other mechanisms that provide randomized virtual items for purchase must disclose the odds of receiving each type of item to customers prior to purchase." (Apple App Store Review Guidelines, sec. 3.1.1, In-App Purchase), they do not enforce this policy. Instead they direct consumers reporting violations to address their complaints to the game publisher directly, whom of course is not going to be inclined to find fault with itself. I know this because I filed a complaint with the Google Play Store on loot boxes available for purchase within an app called Pixel Starships, and got no response at all. I then filed the same complaint directly to Apple reporting the apparent violation of Apple App Store Review Guidelines policy, and the response I got was, "Please know that while iTunes is the vendor of the app, we do not have control on what goes on within the application, the mechanics of the application, or delivery of the content. The iTunes Store simply processes the financial aspect of the transaction on behalf of the developer.". So I did take my concerns regarding the sale of loot boxes up with the developer of Pixel Starships, SavySoda, and this is the response I got from a developer of the game: "At the end of the day, games are designed to keep players engaged for as long as possible in anyway feasible way it can. If anything, the fact that it is used prominently in gambling games just reinforces my point. They're effective in keeping players engaged." Pixel Starships is currently marketed by SavySoda on the Google Play Store as being appropriate for children ages 10 and up. Loot boxes are gambling by definition because they are purchased with a wager made using in-game currency whose real money equivalent valuation can be calculated quantitatively, produce a randomized outcome, in which if you win you get a perceived advantage or faster progress in the game. Game publishers do this for the express purpose of reinforcing addictive behavior, even to the extent of bragging about how "addictive" a game is as a sign of quality. Companies selling known addictive products must be regulated as such. Loot boxes should be classified as gambling, because game developers are shameless, and are currently marketing addiction behavior training to children directly as aggressively as humanly possible.

comment: After reading the proposal, I am fully in support of this policy. It’s about time we hold companies accountable for their deceptive practices. As a low-income consumer, I have to be very careful and attentive when shopping, even my basic needs. Many times I have compared the price I received for a good or service with the price a family or friend received and been disgusted by the differences. This is to be expected in certain arenas, such as insurance, buying a car, or loans. But, groceries, household goods, and other “priced as marked” items and services should not differ. The money I earn should have the same value as any other person’s money. I should be able to reasonably estimate my expenses and plan for them. I believe that requiring businesses to display personalized pricing and inform consumers what data was used to inform those prices is reasonable, but I fear that businesses will do the bare minimum required. I foresee a “specially priced” notification and a generic list of data that “may” have been used to determine that price. That is not transparency. It will allow me the agency to choose business that do not engage in surveillance pricing, but due to consolidation that has been allowed in the US, often there isn’t a competitor to support. The surveillance pricing violation examples presented in this proposal are egregious. Why are companies even allowed to collect some of these variables? Since when does a hotel have a valid need to assess whether a customer has a funeral or other personally important event? Since when have rideshare companies been allowed to collect data about a person’s immediate medical condition? These sound like blatant violations of privacy that, if prosecutes appropriately, would reduce the risk of this data being used against the consumer. We have laws that regulate the kinds of data certain businesses can reasonably collect. Sounds like the first step is to investigate and prosecute companies for their data aggregation strategies. If the Uber app asked if it could access my Google fit data, I would immediately delete the app. Buying the info from a data broker should be illegal and the business should be held accountable for every individual user it violated. I realize the examples were intended to highlight the most objectionable possible offenses. But they also highlight how lax the FTC has been in policing data privacy. I read the privacy policies and would never allow an app to estimate why I was traveling or whether I was having a medical emergency. No app has ever disclosed the variables they estimate based on the data we allow them to collect. That’s what we need to handle next I guess. Jesus. In sum, I support the FTC’s policy to require companies to clearly personalized prices and provide transparency about the data used to determine those prices. Maybe when people see companies are estimating extremely private information about their lives, more will be done to protect our privacy.

comment: I have some different ideas about the exceptions of proposed section 314.6. It talked about exempting some small institutions from several requirements, and the reason for this exemption is that some requirements are too expensive for small institutions to afford. I agree with the idea that this exemption can help institutions which have relatively small amounts of customer information reduce their financial burden, but I think these subsections are also very important for protecting customers' information, so it would be more helpful if we can keep them. Thus, from my perspective, these paragraphs should not be directly exempted. On the contrary, it would be better if the rule makes these exemptions optional for small institutions, which means they can choose whether they will follow these subsections or not according to their own financial situation. The other method that might help small institutions to afford these subsections is that Federal Trade Commission can create a fund to pay these costs for them. If any of the small institutions who gets the fund develops into a larger institution in the future, then these institutions can be required to put money in the fund to help other small institutions protect their customers' information better.

comment: I am submitting this comment as an ordinary consumer. I am not affiliated with any company, trade group, or organization.I believe personalized pricing based on data surveillance is wrong, and that allowing it to continue unchecked puts us on a very slippery slope. But the part that alarms me most is how few people know it is happening at all. Before writing this, I asked my husband, my family, and my friends. Not one of them knew this was going on, or that it was even possible. Every one of them assumed that the price on a website is simply the price, the same number anyone else would see. That assumption is so basic that most people have never thought to question it. What prompted me to look into this was a video I came across in which three people in the same city pulled up the same item on target.com — a can of Spam — and were each shown a different price. The same group repeated the test on Uber, scheduling the same pickup and drop-off for the same date and time, and got wildly different fares. They tried it again booking a hotel, with the same result. Nowhere on any of those sites was there a word telling them the price they were seeing had been shaped by their own data. That omission is the whole problem. If a retailer told me plainly that my price was personalized, I would act differently. I would comparison shop, check another device, clear my browser, look at a competitor — I would not simply accept the first number I was given. Without that disclosure, I do not know there is anything to push back against. Silence is what makes the practice work, and silence is what makes it unfair. This hands corporations an enormous advantage over the average consumer, who has no way to detect it and no idea to look for it. And I have to ask where it ends. If companies can use these methods unrestricted and under the radar, what stops the inputs from expanding? Race. Income. Occupation. Marital status. Number of children. Age. Gender. Spending habits. These are exactly the characteristics we have decided, as a country, that people should not be treated differently on. If consumers are protected from discrimination in the workplace, why should they not have comparable protection at the point of sale? I want to note the scale of public reaction here, because I think it speaks to the deception issue directly. Beyond my own informal polling of the people around me, the video I referenced — posted on tiktok by the account @christheproducer21 — has drawn over 16,600 comments. The overwhelming response is shock and outrage, and, more tellingly, complete unawareness that this was ever happening. When a practice can operate for years without the public having any idea of it, that is strong evidence that it defies reasonable consumer expectations. My position is that this should not be happening at all. If you and your neighbors live in the same city and shop at the same store, the price should be the same across the board. If the Commission concludes it cannot prohibit the practice outright, then at an absolute minimum the disclosure requirement must be real: 1. It must appear where the price appears — on the product page, at the moment I see the number — not buried in a privacy policy or terms of service that no one reads. 2. It must state clearly that the price is personalized, identify the categories of personal data used, and explain how that data affected the price I am being shown. 3. It must be specific enough that an ordinary person can act on it, because a disclosure that does not let me change my behavior is not a disclosure at all. Most people today are juggling more than enough already. They should not also have to worry that the store is quietly sizing them up. I urge the Commission to adopt the strongest possible reading of its Section 5 authority here and to enforce it aggressively. Thank you for the opportunity to comment.
label: Negative

comment: Alcon Vision, LLC, the largest eye care medical device manufacturer in the world and one of the four major manufacturers of contact lenses in the US, appreciates the opportunity to comment on the FTCs Notice of Proposed Rulemaking for the Contact Lens Rule. Alcons mission is to enhance quality of life through innovative products, increase access to quality eye care, as well as drive training and education of eye care professionals (ECPs) with the goal of improving sight around the world. Above all, Alcon is dedicated to promoting and safeguarding the eye health of all patients who benefit from our products. We acknowledge the Commissions objective to update the Contact Lens Rule to address current marketplace practices. Alcon believes an appropriate balance should be achieved that addresses patient safety, consumer choice and industry competition. We offer discrete comments in three areas: lens substitution, passive verification, and prescription release. Lens Substitution (SNPRM, p17 IIB): Alcon strongly advocates for measures that protect the clinical decision-making of ECPs when prescribing lenses, and limit manufacture and/or brand substitution. As highlighted in our April 6, 2018 comments because of differences in contact lens polymers, manufacturing techniques, lens design, optical properties, lens packaging solutions and other variables, not all contact lenses fit the same and therefore are not interchangeable. In addition, some manufactures utilize older lens materials that do not transmit as much oxygen to the eye, which can put patients eye health at risk.(1) Finally, clinical experience demonstrates the power profile (optical power of the contact lens that affects correction of vision) varies by brand, eg, all -3.00 D or +3.00 D lenses (or other power) are not the same. As a result, it is not uncommon for a patient to need one power for a given lens brand and a different power for another this can even occur with two brands from the same manufacturer. Eliminating the ability of a patient to modify the prescription as written by an ECP would ensure proper contact lens fit, optimal visual acuity, lens comfort, and ocular health. Therefore, we suggest the Commission modify the proposal allowing patients to request an alternative contact lens (eg, manufacturer/material), and have patients and sellers always adhere to the prescription written by the ECP. Passive Verification (SNPRM, p17 IIB): The Commissions proposal with respect to prescription verification by telephone fails to adequately address the health and safety risks associated with robocalls; calls (intentional or not) that often undermines the goal of clear and effective communication of the prescription. A verification process that includes a detailed, standardized script, eg, specific terms, requested information, presentation order, and minimum/maximum time limitations of the call, could further accomplish the shared goal of ensuring the verification of a legitimate contact lens prescription. Prescription Release (SNPRM, p15 IIA): Alcon continues to support any effort to improve patient access to their prescription via electronic delivery. We also believe consumers should be able to choose where to purchase their contact lenses. Subsequently, Alcon contact lenses are available for sale by ECPs and at eye care retailers, pharmacies, as well as through mail order and online retailers. Alcon supports the Commissions intent to minimize (or preferably eliminate) the administrative burden placed on the contact lens prescribing ECP. However, in the supplemental notice of proposed rulemaking, the Commission seeks to exempt ECPs who do not have a financial interest in the sale of contact lenses, e.g., those who work in eye care retail locations, from the requirement to obtain a patient prescription acknowledgement. Given the multitude of business relationships, it may be difficult to ascertain when an ECP may or may not have a financial interest in the sale of contact lenses. As a result, to the extent the patient acknowledgment rule is adopted, the rule should be applied to all ECPs regardless of financial interest and whether it is the ECP selling the contact lenses, or the next-door retailer or other seller. In summary, Alcon supports changes to the Contact Lens Rule that balance patient health and safety while at the same time preserving and protecting consumer choice in the evolving US contact lens marketplace. We appreciate the Commissions approach to provide additional clarity that will advance the benchmarks established in the Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act and the goals established by the Commission. Thank you for consideration of our comments. Sincerely, R.E. Weisbarth OD, FAAO, Vice President, Professional AffairsUS Vision Care, Alcon Source: 1. Musgrave CSA, Fang F. Contact Lens Materials: A Materials Science Perspective. Materials (Basel). 2019;12(2):261. Published 2019 Jan 14. doi:10.3390/ma12020261.

comment: There is currently an unreasonably high prevalence of all types of repair restrictions in the United States. Economic stagnation, reduced productivity, and consumer financial duress are the predictable results from all types of repair restrictions. Manufacturers repair restrictions impact small and local businesses the hardestleading to greatly reduced market competitiveness and higher concentrations of market power in larger corporate manufacturers. The market distortions created by manufacturers repair restrictions have caused increased prices for repairing goods to often-times unjustifiably exceed the cost of purchasing a replacement product, thus generating excessive waste from the disposal of otherwise reusable components. The accessibility and timeliness of repairs, and the quality of repairs, are further degraded by manufacturers repair restrictions, as many limitationsboth financially and logisticallymay unduly burden and impair consumers from accessing a manufacturers authorized repair service. Independent repair shops and consumers ability to repair warrantied products are effectively marginalized into near impossibility by manufacturers repair restrictions, unless the owner of the device in question is willing to void the warranty or to risk other forms of retaliation by manufacturersin particular, the use of so-called Digital Rights Management (DRM) allows manufacturers to legally accuse independent repair shops and consumers of violating the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA). Consumers and independent repair shops risk possible legal retaliatory actions under the DMCA simply for trying to repair a device, if repairs for certain devices unjustly require circumventing DRM restrictions embedded within certain devices by manufacturersand manufacturers often embed DRM in devices solely for the purpose of unjustly monopolizing the repair process. Manufacturers have no legitimate justifications for repair restrictions, or for using DRM to monopolize the repair process. The only basis for such supposed justifications is to further corporate profit by anti-competitive means, including furthering the sale of services, extended warranties, or entirely new replacement devices by manufacturersand thus generating unnecessary waste, by unduly shortening product life cycles through artificial repair restrictions. The are no legitimate risks to the general welfare or public posed by repairs made by consumers or independent repair shops, but instead only benefitsbenefits such as increasing competition in the broader marketplace, encouraging new market participants to enter the repair business, decreasing monopolistic tendencies, increasing market productivity, and further benefiting the environment by reducing waste from the unnecessary early replacement of devices. Any liability faced by manufacturers when consumers, or independent repair workers, are injured while repairing a product (or injured after using or coming into contact with a product that has been repaired improperly), can be mitigated and indemnified by an act of Congress or by rule-making at the regulatory level, and is therefore not a legitimate business concern, but is rather an anti-competitive ruse used by manufacturers to attempt to maintain market dominance and to crowd-out competitors. Further, consumersor, more properly, the property owners of the chattel in question for repairmost often do not understand the existence of repair restrictions, and the effects lead to potentially unjustifiable legal liability for consumers after simply trying to repair their own personal possessionsespecially in the presence of DRM. Consumers also do not understand the potential repercussions if they face prosecution under the DMCA for repairing their own personal devices that have DRM embedded into their property (as the device to be repaired is the chattel of the property owner, and so the consumer is also a property owner in this regard). Finally, repairs made by consumers, or by independent repair shops, should be considered to be covered by the 9th Amendments protection of unenumerated rights, as manufacturers repair restrictions deny or disparage [rights] retained by the people to repair their own personal possessions. The right to repair personal possessions (or chattel) surely existed both before and after the ratification of the Constitution, and should therefore properly be viewed within the light of the 9th Amendmentespecially, when considering that the right to repair such goods and chattels has only become encumbered within recent times by the relatively new anti-competitive practice of repair restrictions.

comment: Ballad Health's forthcoming merger of Mountain States/Indian Path hospital and Wellmont/Holston Valley hospital has been and continues to be nothing short of a disaster. Holston Valley, Kingsport, TN is a Level 1 trauma hospital servicing East Tennessee and Southwest Virginia. It is the closest hospital by air and ground transportation for Southwest Virginia and several East Tennessee counties. The merger reduces the Level 1 status to a Level 3 Plus closes the hospital's much needed NICU. Johnson City Medical Center will be the only Level 1 trauma hospital and the Niswonger Childrens hospital will be the primary NICU. The downgrade is absurb considering Eastman and Domtar are within a 2 to 10 minutes drive. The "golden hour" is called such for a very good reason. By making Johnson City Medical Center the sole Level 1 hospital, ground and air transport times have been gravely increased resulting in deaths. An exuberant number of doctors, speciality surgeons and nurses have left leaving the ER and hospital gravely understaffed resulting in ER wait time to as much as 12 hours. General surgeons must now be trained and trauma certified by October 1st. Patients are being discharged early to have available beds. Patients have been moved to Indian Path to free up beds. (NOTE: Insurance will not pay for the unnecessary transport. Too, insurance companies rejecting claims of patients being taken to Johnson City rather than a the much closer Holston Valley.) The merger of assets originally set for July 1 has been moved to October 1. In addition to these medical issues, Ballad Health's appointed Board of Directors is composed of "conflicts of interest" people. These Directors are making decisions which by no means are for the betterment of citizens. Not one person representing everyday citizens is on the Board. It is in the best interest of citizens to replace the Board with a citizens authoritative system.

comment: As a practicing ophthalmologist, I am deeply concerned about proposals included in the Federal Trade Commission's proposed amendments to the Contact Lens Rule. Proposed: 1. Acknowledge receipt of the contact lens prescription by signing a separate confirmation statement; 2. Sign a prescriber-retained copy of the prescription that contains a statement confirming the patient has received it; 3. Sign a prescriber-retained copy of the sales receipt for the examination that contains a statement confirming the patient received the prescription; or 4. Be provided with a digital copy of the prescription, and retaining evidence that it was sent, received, or made accessible, downloadable, and printable. While I would welcome changes to the Contact Lens Rule that prioritize patient safety, the prescription-receipt verification process and three-year record hold places an unfair burden on ophthalmology practices. There is no evidence that our patients do not have adequate access to the contact lens records. Such an administrative burden should not be placed on small businesses that are already going to great lengths to comply with the Contact Lens Rule. We appreciate the FTC's effort in trying to alleviate additional burdens on physician practices by suggesting multiple avenues through which prescribers could comply with new requirements, the proposed changes will still place financial and administrative burdens on ophthalmology practices. I strongly urge the FTC to withdraw this latest proposed change to the Contact Lens Rule. There is no benefit to the patient's safety with these burdensome rules. Thank you for your consideration. Robert M. Scharf, M.D.

The local and state legislators are in Ballad's bag, and the local boards of our government are in Ballad's bag, and we are having little response from our news media on this. I would like to point out that Rusty Crowe, hand carried and got passed a bill in favor of Ballad to oversee itself, with anyone questioning this must pay for anything relating to a challenge in court. Now, Rusty Crowe is also on Ballad's payroll;;; Corruption at it's worst. We have near 20m signatures protesting and against this merger. The COPA was supposed to be an oversight to check and make sure no healthcare was downgraded in our area. I have been to two copa meetings and they cannot help. It is a disgrace. This merger should be stopped immediately before it destroys all the healthcare that we have left. I have addressed this to the local and state boards via emails and letters, and no one has answered or done anything. I also mailed my opinion to Frontline, 48 hours, 60 minutes, and NBC Dateline for their input on an investigation of the corruption that has happened in this merger. I am also requesting you guys to look into this matter, and do an investigation, and you will see first hand the corruption that has taken place in the downgrading and eroding of our healthcare in northeast Tn. and southwest, Va. Thank you very much. My name is Gary Hooker, and I am 72 years old, and my phone number is 423-361-2057, and I live in the area being downgraded. Thanks.

comment: Requiring eye doctors to obtain and store additional documentation from contact lens wearers is not only burdensome, but also misdirected regulation. It is obvious that those proposing such regulations have dollar signs in their eyes. They have the sole objective of selling more and more contact lenses. Unfortunately, this is at the expense of the patients' visual health and will do nothing to improve it. This regulation will only add financial burdens on providers, which unnecessarily will raise eye care cost for patients. It is truly a distraction for addressing what most eye care physicians consider to be a major concern with the contact lens industry - the blatant disregard for patient health from illegal online contact lens sales. I urge you to focus on the true threat at hand. Please do more to help us preserve our patients' eye health, not to help online retailers make more money. Regards, Michael Peterson, OD

comment: July 30, 2019 To Whom It May Concern: Many physicians, including myself, pursued this career because we love helping people and want to make a difference. We hate feeling like we are too late to have the kind of impact our patients really need. But here in Northeast Tennessee and Southwest Virginia, we face that feeling all too often. As a primary care physician who serves in both a Ballad Health Medical Associates practice and as the medical director of Providence Medical Clinic, which provides free healthcare to people in need, I do everything I can to set people on a course for better health. Unfortunately, I cannot undo decades of poor lifestyle choices with their diets, activity levels, and addictions. As a result, many of my patients, especially those at Providence Medical Clinic, dont just suffer from a single illness or ailment. They have chronic, major issues such as behavioral health conditions, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, obesity and lung disease from tobacco use. With the formation of Ballad, we are now able to focus more of our efforts on issues of health which are plaguing our region in order to make a lasting impact on our patients. With our renewed focus on population health issues in our region, true culture change is more likely to occur. In the 18 months since Ballad Healths launch, our medical care is regularly recognized among the top of our region and nation, and we have done tremendous work in improving access to primary care, hospital services and specialist medicine. Ballad Health was also among the first 30 organizations in the nation and the only one spanning two states to create an Accountable Care Community, a collaborative group that consists of more than 200 individual organizations with more than 250 representatives who have joined forces to improve community health, knowing to do so involves efforts aimed at educational success and economic opportunity. The ACC aligns efforts from all sectors of our communities and region. Working together, we are focused on addressing the upstream causes of chronic disease and other health problems. Those causes are not always immediately apparent, but we do know exposure to Adverse Childhood Experiences, also known as social traumas, increases the risk for alcohol and drug abuse, depression, smoking and suicide, all of which are obvious health concerns. They also raise the chances for unsafe sexual practices, poor work and academic performance, domestic and sexual violence and financial stress, which can also have negative impacts on health. Many of our regions health issues can be traced to multi-generational struggles with these issues. The goal of the ACC, then, as well as so many of Ballad Healths programs and initiatives, is to reduce these high-risk health behaviors before they have a chance to damage our next generations health and well-being. Beyond that, we have resolved to do something just as vital: to listen. After all, if Ballad Health is to be a strong advocate in addressing the tough problems our region faces, we need to put additional effort into listening to our population about what they have experienced and what they need. The world is full of suffering, but it is also full of overcoming. That is why I support Ballad Healths initiatives and efforts because through the work we are doing together, we can help our region overcome so much. Sincerely, Marta J Wayt, DO, FACP

comment: As a gamer let me tell you, loot boxes have gotten out of control in the last 3-5 years. The gaming community has tried for years and years to get them under control. We have repeatedly warned developers and publishers that if they do not self-regulate and learn to control their runaway greed in regards to loot boxes that the government will eventually have to step in and regulate loot boxes for them. They chose not listen and so here we are. When possible I like to avoid needless government regulation. I believe the government should only step in when two conditions are met. First, when people or corporations have shown they lack the ability to, or are unwilling to, self-regulate. Second, when there is a genuine and growing harm done by not regulating. The first is unquestionably true. Gaming companies have time and time again expanded loot box systems, made them more predatory, and even done what they could to specifically target children with them. They have done everything possible to make them more profitable without even considering the affect these things are having on anyone, including children. I believe the second condition has been met as well. Game companies have spent years analyzing data on how people interact with loot boxes. They've perfectly tweaked them to give you just enough to keep you spending money but not enough to ever be happy. They are designed to be addictive and it is having a very negative affect on children. Children are simply not mentally equipped with the necessary tools to avoid targeted addiction at this level. Even some adults find themselves falling prey to loot boxes. With all that in mind I would like to propose some ideas on how to regulate loot boxes. First and most critically of all, we need to ban game companies from selling loot boxes to anyone under 18. For the most part I do not have a problem with adults having access to them much like I do not have a problem with adults gambling. Although even some adults can't handle gambling or loot boxes which leads me to my next idea. Currently, on the back of every lottery ticket are hotlines for gambling addiction. This can act as a critical life preserver to someone with an addiction problem. I believe that games that want to sell loot boxes need to include phone numbers and/or site URLs for gambling addiction help on the back of their boxes. In closing I just want to say that I'm glad that someone is finally willing to step in and look into this growing problem. The advent of the internet and gaming has brought many great wonders to our society but it's important that we step in where appropriate and help guide new technology and experiences to the best version of themselves. Thank you for your time and I hope something I wrote here today helps when making your final decision.

comment: Dear Chairman Simons, I am a small town Private Practice Optometrist from the Heartland of America... Indiana. Why does our National Government and its agencies love to operate with NO common sense? We already have a law (the 2003 Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act) that every OD I know follows. It says we have to release the contact lens prescription to our patients at the end of a complete Eye Exam. It is simple and it allows patients to buy there contacts where ever they want. I agree with that Law, we should all be allowed to shop our free market! But your FTC is now looking into forcing more regulation onto every Eyecare provider. For what gain?? Who is being hurt by the current law? Why does our government seem to love looking for problems that don't exist and then come up with a plan to solve those imaginary problems? I can only assume it is somehow either a financial gain for some agency or it is to make an agency look like they are doing something productive..... Like they are "earning" their money? These new regulations, like many "laws" seem to have good intentions, but they only create even more paperwork, time and expense for our offices. Time that we would much rather spend taking care of our patients and expenses that we would much rather NOT have to pass on to our patients! So if the intention is to "protect" citizens' rights..... I would argue that those rights are already well protected with current law and these new proposals will only burden the citizens with less time with their doctor and with higher cost of care to see their doctors!! As a 22 year practicing Optometrist, I call for you, Chairman Simons, to OPEN YOUR EYES and SEE..... See with 20/20 Clarity.... how these new regulations are seriously NOT NEEDED. See how citizens will NOT gain any protection from these regulations, See how these regulations will actually cause more harm to citizens. Do NOT be Myopic and focus on the short term gain of seeming important by passing a new "good sounding" regulation..... Don't be blinded by an imaginary problem! You could truly help the citizens, and save a lot of Tax money, by simply dropping any more discussion of these burdensome, costly, unnecessary, regulations. Let them die in the peace and silence of non-discussion. May COMMON SENSE be used once again in America!! David Hyndman, O.D. (Citizen)

comment: On behalf of National Taxpayers Unions (NTU) thousands of supporters across the country, I am honored to submit the attached comments in PDF form on the Federal Trade Commissions (FTC) upcoming Hearing on Competition and Consumer Protection in the 21st Century, focusing on privacy issues. Consumer data privacy regulations are an issue of particular importance to Americans right now, but governments across the globe have been taking massive anti-consumer steps in overregulating how the government treats private data. National Taxpayers Union has been warning against European-style data regulations for years, and we have recently seen the damage that can be done when the European Union instituted its General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Secretary of Commerce Wilbur Ross stated the GDPR has made the EU less competitive and closed off the ability of many EU companies to do business internationally. GDPR has also killed off a number of small businesses that did not have the resources or the staffing capabilities to comply with the new regulations. A light-touch regulatory regime has worked well for Americans for decades, and the FTC would be forward-thinking to continue this approach. As NTU commented to the FTC in August, the tendency to overregulate can not only impact consumers in negative ways, it can also adversely affect taxpayers. It is the taxpayers interest in privacy regulation that the longer-form comment document we have uploaded and submitted with this description will address in further detail.

It will give companies a loophole to legally discriminate against buyers under the guise of "informed consent." Real consumer protection means stopping this unfair practice entirely, not just making us sign a form agreeing to it. Please protect regular people and ban algorithmic surveillance pricing.

comment: As a practicing ophthalmologist, I am deeply concerned about proposals included in the Federal Trade Commission's proposed amendments to the Contact Lens Rule. While I would welcome changes to the Contact Lens Rule that prioritize patient safety, the prescription-receipt verification process and three-year record hold places an unfair burden on ophthalmology practices. It is also medically inappropriate. Contact lens patients need regular examinations at least once per year and this three year period would allow patients to skip this essential examination process and expose them to medical risks. As a corneal subspecialist I have seen the complications some of which are vision threatening that result from patient abuse and self treatment. Contact lenses are not like a pair of shoes. The eye even in cases of longstanding contact lens wear can break down and become permanently damaged from unsupervised contact lens wear. This new burden is also unwarranted, as there is little evidence that ophthalmologists are not in compliance with the existing Contact Lens Rule. Such an administrative burden should not be placed on small businesses that are already going to great lengths to comply with the Contact Lens Rule and do so despite serious concerns with the current prescription-verification system that we believe puts our patients at risk. While we appreciate the FTC's effort in trying to alleviate additional burdens on physician practices by suggesting multiple avenues through which prescribers could comply with new requirements, the proposed changes will still place financial and administrative burdens on ophthalmology practices. I strongly urge the FTC to withdraw its latest proposed changes to the Contact Lens Rule and focus on efforts to enhance patient safety. If not physician prescribers will continue to decrease their role in contact lens prescribing and management. Thank you for your consideration.

comment: Dear Chairman Simons, I am a doctor of optometry providing primary eye health and vision care in our local community. For more than two years, my fellow eye doctors and I, and the patients and communities we serve with dedication, have faced the threat of a seriously flawed Federal Trade Commission (FTC) plan to impose massive new costs and far-reaching new requirements on all contact lens prescribing. The proposal, even in its latest form, will divert precious resources away from the care and innovation at the heart of my practice and cast public doubt on the integrity of optometrists and ophthalmologists, our para-professional staff and other employees. It should be withdrawn once again, and re-worked to put the interests of patients, doctors, and public health and safety first. Its especially notable that the FTCs actions remain at odds with the policy direction being pursued by Congress and Federal agencies to prioritize the elimination of burdensome, costly and unjustified mandates in health care, especially those that are overwhelming small and mid-sized health practices on the frontlines of care. Here are active examples that I hope the agency is aware of: -Merit Based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) Special Considerations for Small Practices: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) developed the framework for MIPS acknowledging the regulatory burden that health care providers already are facing. Considering that reality, CMS reduced the number of clinicians that are required to participate. CMS supported this effort out of the agencys desire to give physicians more time with their patients, not computers. Additionally, CMS is mindful of the unique challenges that face smaller physician practices and added new bonus points for clinicians caring for patients in those settings. -Patients over Paperwork: CMS initiated this regulatory review in 2017 aimed at removing regulatory obstacles that get in the way of providers spending time with patients. -Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA): Currently, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) is considering eliminating or modifying the requirement for covered health care providers to make a good faith effort to obtain individuals written acknowledgment of receipt of providers Notice of Privacy Practices. The stated aim of this potential change is to reduce burden and free up resources for covered entities to devote to coordinated care. More than 100 U.S. Senators and House members weighed-in against the FTCs original proposal. And now, since the May 2019 release of the Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rule Making, more than 25 U.S. Senators have registered their continued concern with the Commissions proposed new requirements, stating that the FTCs reaffirmation of a prescription release confirmation proposal is both unnecessary and overly burdensome. According to the FTCs own data, few complaints regarding prescription release have been received and the Commission estimates that this new mandate would add millions in new regulatory compliance costs. It is especially troubling that the Commissions stated intent is to gain new investigative authority to target small and mid-sized independent medical practices serving communities in our state and across the country. As I understand it, the purpose of the ten-year review of the Contact Lens Rule is to assess its effectiveness based on a thorough, fact-based analysis and a process free of bias, false claims and insider-influenced policy. Doctors, like me, and our patients across the United States who are continuing to live and work under your agencys threat of baseless and punishing regulations look forward to participating in open and thoughtful discussions, including through the meetings we have been seeking with you and your fellow commissioners. Michael Murphy, O.D.

comment: Forcing people to only use the vendors repair service is way to limiting! First not every can get to the limited number of service centers the vendor offers. A good example is the Apple butterfly keyboards which fail instead of a design which offered a removable sub assembly from the main case its riveted in! Just look at the amount of energy (carbon cost) it takes to make a new phone as an example vs just replacing the sub component that failed saving the delta difference! So as you can see its much bigger than a small part its also the amount of waste and energy! While my focus here is on computer and phone repair there are other industries like farm equipment where repairs are time sensitive! Having a dead combine in the middle of harvest doesn't help the farmer where he needs to truck the unit to the dealer which could be a 100 miles away! A gamer might have the skills to service the unit in the field if he had the diagnostic decoder ring and the ability to switch out parts. Again, safety is not the risk its the lost of the harvest that is! If safety is such an issue then why haven't the vendors jumped to self healing battery technology which is available? comment: Franchise Rule Regulatory Review, 16 CFR part 436, Matter No. R511003 There is a continuing need for the Rule because the whole reason behind this Rule was to protect the interests and assets of prospective franchise purchasers. Buying a franchise costs a lot of money, and they will be met with consequences that will make lasting impact, so having such an extensive disclosure process is only beneficial to help prospective franchise purchasers reduce information asymmetry and enable them to make a more informed disclosure. The Rule was recently amended to reduce the inconsistency in reporting between states, but there was a concern that this might also compromise on the amount of information that will be provided to prospective franchise purchasers. In my opinion, the amount of historical and financial information is very necessary, but not enough. Purchasing a franchise goes beyond just the historical and financial data there are other factors that are critical in considering the purchase of a franchise, such as reputation, especially on media. These franchises depend so much on reputation and that is beyond what historical and financial numbers can portray; therefore, there should be an analysis regarding the success of its marketing efforts be it on social media, traditional media, or non-traditional media, and include the franchises main issues in terms of brand image, and what they are aiming to achieve. With franchises, it is often a challenge to keep their image consistent since they are owned by different people, but brand image affects the success of the business so much that I think it is necessary to take into account one of the most essential factors needed to build trust with future customers.

comment: I am a doctor of optometry providing primary eye health and vision care in our local community. It has come to my attention that a call to your colleagues was distributed last week that requested support for a letter regarding the FTCs contact lens proposal. It is my opinion that this effort will be harmful to the doctor-patient relationship, and create unnecessary burdens in the practice of eye and vision care, therefore I urge you to NOT sign-on to a letter proposed by Attorneys General Miller, Peterson, Stein, and Reyes. I agree that it is important that consumers be given a genuine opportunity to exercise choice in the contact lens market. However, before one considers offering support for far reaching government regulations to be imposed on small businesses, its important to know the true state of the contact lens market as the market has changed tremendously since the Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act was passed. o Lens prices are competitive: The AOA conducted a price comparison analysis in which they compared online retailer cost vs the average in-office cost to determine the dollar price difference and percent change in price for 81 different contact lenses. Of the 81 lenses studied, 28 were more expensive online, while 53 were more expensive in the doctors office. Across all lenses included in the AOAs price comparison analysis, there was an average price difference of just $0.32 o Patients Have More Retailer Options than Ever: The fastest growing distribution channel for contact lens sales in the USA was the online / Internet channel. In 2017, online retailers generated $786 million in salesgrowing by 4.9% during the 12 month ending period Dec17 and growing by 11.1% over the 24 monthending period Dec17. o There is Widespread Agreement that the Current Rule is Working: The CEO of 1-800-CONTACTS itself acknowledged that the current rule is working in a March 2018 FTC workshop noting, The FCLCA and CLR have succeeded in encouraging greater competition and choice in the contact lens marketplace. Consumers today have more choice and more convenience. The competitive benefits have gone beyond price. I think that the FTC can consider this a successful rule. Doctors of optometry are concerned with the FTCs claims regarding non-compliance of prescription release requirements. Despite disagreeing with the accusation regarding compliance, the profession has offered an alternative to the signed acknowledgement proposal put forward by the Commission. The proposal supported by optometry would require all contact lens prescribers to post signage in their offices notifying patients of their right to their contact lens prescription. This is a less burdensome and less intrusive approach than the proposal put forward by the FTC. This approach would also do more to broadly educate consumers. In all, through letters, direct exchanges during committee hearings and committee report language, more than 100 Members of Congress Republicans and Democrats -- have spoken out against the FTCs misguided approach to updating the contact lens rule and called on the agency to prioritize a crackdown on illegal device sales, including those being reported on by the national media -- https://www.nytimes.com/2019/07/21/business/media/hubble-contact-lens.html. And now, since the May 2019 release of the Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rule Making, more than 25 U.S. Senators have registered their continued concern with the Commissions proposed new requirements, stating that the FTCs reaffirmation of a prescription release confirmation proposal is both unnecessary and overly burdensome. According to the FTCs own data, few complaints regarding prescription release have been received and the Commission estimates that this new mandate would add millions in new regulatory compliance costs. It is especially troubling that the Commissions stated intent is to gain new investigative authority to target small and mid-sized independent medical practices serving communities in our state and across the country. As I understand it, the purpose of the ten-year review of the Contact Lens Rule is to assess its effectiveness based on a thorough, fact-based analysis and a process free of bias, false claims and insider-influenced policy. Doctors, like me, and our patients across the United States who are continuing to live and work under FTCs threat of baseless and punishing regulations look forward to participating in open and thoughtful discussions at both the state and federal level.

comment: Requiring a signature from patients, even in these modified ways still creates an atmosphere of distrust and implication of dishonesty. Why would I need to get the signature of my patient to confirm they received a prescription unless I was doing something wrong that required the proof. We are required to give glasses prescriptions every time we refract a patient and generate a prescription but don't get a signed verification. In the hospital I work we have a pharmacy and sell medications but I don't get a signed verification I gave the patient a written script so they could get their medications at the pharmacy of their choice. The fact is we are caring for our patients and are expected to act in a professional and ethical manner. Second, the process is a burden on those using an electronic record. Having a signature pad in every exam room for patients to sign they received a prescription so it can be verified or having a patient sign a duplicate copy of their script then scan it back into the EMR, creates a burden, not only a financial burden but one of time. The amount of patients ordering their own contacts has steadily grown over the past number of years and with the advertising seen for online contact sales, both online and on TV I just don't see how there is such a large problem requiring a signature from every contact lens patient. We are creating more of a problem with these new rules. If the issue is patients truly not understanding they have the right to obtain a prescription for contacts, allow that language to be spelled out in the entry forms a patient signs when they check in. Require signage in the exam room or waiting room etc. There are other ways of tackling this issue besides getting in the way of the doctor patient relationship by implying their doctor is doing something wrong requiring the patient to verify a prescription was given.
